Drop D and Open D chord charts

Drop D and Open D both lower the 6th string to D, so chords in the key of D get a deep low root. Drop D changes only one string, so most standard shapes still work. Open D changes four strings, so the open strings ring as a D major chord.

Drop D (D A D G B E)

Lower only the 6th string:

  • 6th string: E → D (down 2 semitones)

A quick check: the 6th string at the 7th fret should sound the same as the open 5th string (A). Chord shapes on the top five strings are the same as in standard tuning; only chords that use the 6th string change. The open 6th, 5th, and 4th strings make a D5 power chord, so one finger across those strings at any fret plays a power chord.

Open D (D A D F# A D)

From standard tuning, change four strings. The 5th and 4th strings stay the same.

  • 6th string: E → D (down 2 semitones)
  • 3rd string: G → F# (down 1 semitone)
  • 2nd string: B → A (down 2 semitones)
  • 1st string: E → D (down 2 semitones)

The open strings ring as D. As in Open G, one finger (or a slide) across all strings at a fret plays a major chord: the 5th fret is G and the 7th fret is A, the I, IV, and V chords of D.

Which one should I use?

  • Drop D if you want a heavier low end but still play mostly standard shapes — common in rock and for songs in D.
  • Open D for slide guitar and for ringing open-string sounds in folk and fingerstyle. Minor chords take more effort, because the open strings are major.
  • DADGAD sits in between: it is Open D with the 3rd string at G instead of F#. See DADGAD chords.
